v2_s1a.what_it_shows: A man, a sack of grain, and a shoe, with a caption about the seller not wanting grain.
v2_s1a.missing: A shoe seller refusing the offered grain with a crossed-out exchange arrow.

v2_s1s.what_it_shows: Two traders holding wheat and cloth, with thought bubbles showing what each wants.
v2_s1s.missing: An after-trade picture showing the farmer with 8 kg wheat remaining plus 1 metre of acquired cloth.
v2_s1s.point: Barter leaves wheat plus acquired cloth

v2_s1b.what_it_shows: Two people with a wheat sack between them; subtitle says selling then buying is not barter.
v2_s1b.missing: Side-by-side exchanges: wheat directly for cloth versus wheat sold for money, then money used to buy cloth.
v2_s1b.point: Barter is direct exchange without money; Selling then buying with money is not barter; Direct exchange identifies barter

v2_s2.what_it_shows: A person beside a handshake and green check mark, suggesting agreement.
v2_s2.missing: Two people exchanging services without cash, with both agreeing on their equal value.
v2_s2.point: No money does not mean free; Services can be bartered too; Both parties decide the value

v2_s3.what_it_shows: Two people holding shopping baskets, with a Hindi subtitle about swapping.
v2_s3.missing: A reciprocal exchange of different needed goods, alongside a separate purchase using money.
v2_s3.point: Barter survives from early civilizations; Matching needs enable moneyless exchange; Money and barter can coexist

v2_s4s.what_it_shows: Two traders hold wheat and money, each thinking of the other item with a question mark.
v2_s4s.missing: A rejected wheat-for-cloth trade beside two separate money-based sales and purchases.
v2_s4s.point: Wheat हर cloth seller को नहीं चाहिए; Barter में दोनों की चाह मिलनी चाहिए; Money से बेचने और खरीदने वाले अलग

v2_s4b.what_it_shows: Grain sacks, one crossed out, a July 17 calendar, and an arrow from grain to a bin.
v2_s4b.missing: A side-by-side barter-versus-money repayment timeline showing grain spoiling and money buying less later.
v2_s4b.point: Barter में मूल्य, विभाजन, भंडारण और repayment की बाधाएँ; Money में debt स्पष्ट, purchasing power अनिश्चित; Barter की बाधाएँ matching से repayment तक

v2_s5a.what_it_shows: Two people exchanging cloth and wheat, illustrating barter.
v2_s5a.missing: A timeline showing barter followed by coins, notes and digital payments.

v2_s5s.what_it_shows: Buyer and seller at a stall with ₹300 goods, ₹500 payment and ₹200 change labels.
v2_s5s.missing: A two-step salt barter exchange linking different wants, followed by payment in metal coins and counting the coins left.
v2_s5s.point: Salt mediates two exchanges; Commodity money bridges different wants; Metal coins pay; remaining coins can be counted

v2_s5b.what_it_shows: Six-stage money timeline above a QR-code payment between buyer and seller, with deposit indicators.
v2_s5b.missing: Linked bank accounts showing existing deposits moving via UPI, alongside coexisting cash and a card holding no money.
v2_s5b.point: Intermediaries ease exchange; UPI moves existing deposits; Forms coexist; cards need not contain money; Recall the book's six-stage ordering

v2_s6.what_it_shows: Comparison table of intrinsic and extrinsic money value, highlighting inherent worth and acceptability.
v2_s6.missing: Gold remaining useful after rejection as payment, beside a rejected currency note with no other use.
v2_s6.point: Two sources of payment value; Utility survives loss of monetary acceptance; Material versus external backing

v2_s7s.what_it_shows: Two men holding salt packets, with questioning thought bubbles outside a shop.
v2_s7s.missing: Salt being sprinkled into a cooking pot to show its use beyond payment.

v2_s7b.what_it_shows: Salt offered between people, with another salt bag pointing to a bowl of food.
v2_s7b.missing: A clear comparison showing salt used both to buy goods and to season food.
v2_s7b.point: Salt has value beyond payment; Usefulness and purchasing power are insufficient separately; Outside-payment usefulness is essential

v2_s8a.what_it_shows: Table linking salt, cattle and cowries to regions or communities; small cowrie-shell illustration.
v2_s8a.missing: A map showing all five commodities’ regions, with cowries being accepted in a payment exchange.
v2_s8a.point: Salt ke regions; cattle ki communities; Cowries: regions aur payment mein acceptance; Tea bricks aur tobacco ke alag regions

v2_s8s.what_it_shows: Two balanced scales link 10 kg grain to 2 kg salt, then salt to cloth.
v2_s8s.missing: A clear three-way equivalence showing 10 kg grain = 2 kg salt = a specified quantity of cloth.
v2_s8s.point: Three quantities have equal assumed value; Salt bridges grain and cloth exchanges

v2_s8b.what_it_shows: Table of commodity money and regions, with salt, cattle and cooking icons.
v2_s8b.missing: An exchange diagram showing salt accepted between traders with mismatched wants, alongside its use in cooking.
v2_s8b.point: Salt bridges mismatched wants; Commodities retain uses beyond payment; Usefulness plus local acceptance enables exchange

v2_s9s.what_it_shows: Grain sack with 100 kg crossed out and 90 kg remaining, linked to a July 17 payment date.
v2_s9s.missing: A spoiled portion of grain beside the reduced sack.
v2_s9s.point: Spoilage leaves less grain for later payment

v2_s9b.what_it_shows: Different-sized cows, a crossed-out standards scroll, and checking and bargaining icons.
v2_s9b.missing: A trade scene showing unequal cattle values and the extra cost of transporting and storing them.
v2_s9b.point: Commodity money has physical limitations; Variation and missing standards complicate trade; Handling problems add payment and storage costs

v4_s1a.what_it_shows: Two people, one holding a ₹100 note, and a grain sack; subtitles question its value, gold backing and legal acceptance.
v4_s1a.missing: A diagram linking ₹100 to how much rice it buys, gold backing, and legal acceptance.
v4_s1a.point: Purchasing power, gold backing, and legal status questioned

v4_s1s.what_it_shows: Two people at a bank counter with gold labeled '1 gram gold' and a note labeled '1 note'.
v4_s1s.missing: An arrow showing the note being returned to the bank in exchange for gold.
v4_s1s.point: Gold-backed notes could be redeemed for gold

v4_s1b.what_it_shows: Paper document, handshake, receipt and shopping basket under a gold-backed currency heading.
v4_s1b.missing: A low-value paper note exchanged for gold through a redemption promise, contrasted with gold reserves offering no redemption claim.
v4_s1b.point: Paper has little material value; redemption gives value; Gold reserves alone do not give holders claims; Redemption promise explains the need for backing

v4_s2s.what_it_shows: A bank with ten numbered gold bars, ten numbered notes, and a small extra note.
v4_s2s.missing: An extra note paired with one extra gold bar labeled 1 gram.
v4_s2s.point: One extra note needs one extra gram

v4_s2b.what_it_shows: Vault, gold reserves pointing to a promise document, and a separate banknote icon; text says redemption in principle.
v4_s2b.missing: A linked diagram showing gold reserves backing notes, limited gold redemption, and falling reserves reducing confidence.
v4_s2b.point: Reserves support the gold promise; Gold backs issue and qualified redemption; Weaker repayment capacity undermines confidence

v4_s3.what_it_shows: Receipt scroll, official stamp, banknotes, and a crossed-out note; Sweden 1661 label.
v4_s3.missing: An arrowed timeline linking deposit receipts to state-issued claims, compulsory acceptance in 1275, and Sweden’s banknotes in 1661.
v4_s3.point: Receipts introduce different monetary milestones; Deposited-value claims gain a state issuer; Compulsory acceptance precedes Sweden's banknotes

v4_s4s.what_it_shows: A shopper outside a grocery store with a ₹100 note displayed.
v4_s4s.missing: A shopkeeper accepting the note, then using it to pay another seller.
v4_s4s.point: Acceptance rests on trust in spending again

v4_s4b.what_it_shows: Government building, handshake for public trust, and a document labeled gold-backed paper.
v4_s4b.missing: A comparison showing fiat backed by authority and trust versus paper redeemable for gold, with central-bank controls on fiat issuance.
v4_s4b.point: Authority and trust give fiat money value; Gold-backed paper is not necessarily fiat; How is issuance controlled without gold?

v4_s5.what_it_shows: Dollar, euro and yen banknotes linked by arrows to a yuan symbol.
v4_s5.missing: A flow diagram showing authority and trust backing money, authorised release after printing, and delayed demand changes after credit changes.
v4_s5.point: Fiat value rests on authority and trust; Printing is not authorised circulation; Credit conditions affect demand with a lag

v4_s6s.what_it_shows: Two people at a grocery shop, one holding a basket; Hindi subtitles discuss valid coins.
v4_s6s.missing: A payment diagram showing debt cleared by valid coins, including special-design coins, with unlimited notes versus a capped coin amount.
v4_s6s.point: Valid payment extinguishes the debt; Special-design valid coins also pay; Notes unlimited; coin acceptance has a limit

v4_s6b.what_it_shows: Banknote icons, denominations and an arrow under a no-total-ceiling heading.
v4_s6b.missing: A side-by-side payment scene showing unlimited valid banknotes accepted but coins accepted only up to a marked limit.
v4_s6b.point: Official recognition and everyday circulation; Valid banknotes have no total tender ceiling; Compulsory coin acceptance stops at a limit

v4_s7a.what_it_shows: Commemorative coin icon with fiat, legal-tender, metal-value and collector-value symbols.
v4_s7a.missing: A collector coin set in a display case contrasted with a coin being spent, with legal-tender and fiat status marked.
v4_s7a.point: Legal tender need not always be fiat; Commemorative coins have distinct status and values; Collector sets are preserved rather than routinely spent

v4_s7s.what_it_shows: Two people at a kirana shop, a crossed-out coin, and captions listing coin tender limits.
v4_s7s.missing: Coin groups with separate tender-limit markers, plus a rejected invalid-coin payment leaving the balance due unchanged.
v4_s7s.point: अमान्य coins से बकाया नहीं मिटता; Coin groups की अलग tender limits

v4_s7b.what_it_shows: Denomination-specific legal-tender limit table, 50-paise and 25-paise coins, and a ₹10 limit label.
v4_s7b.missing: A payment example showing different coin counts with equal total value, alongside separate legal-tender status and collector-price labels.
v4_s7b.point: Limits measure value, not coin count; Different denominations have different status; Payment limit and collector price do not change status

v4_s8.what_it_shows: 2024 label, mining laptop linked to network rules, price tag, and government fixed-value promise icon.
v4_s8.missing: A 2024–2025 comparison showing privately created Bitcoin, market pricing, and mandatory acceptance changing to voluntary use.
v4_s8.point: Bitcoin payment does not prove government issuance; Legal tender exception with non-government creation and pricing; 2025 removes compulsion, not voluntary use

v4_s9.what_it_shows: ₹100 coin, smaller silver coin icon, and a magnifying glass labelled condition.
v4_s9.missing: One coin branching to fixed ₹100 face value and a higher collector market price.
v4_s9.point: One coin, two roles; Face value differs from market price; Collector premium leaves denomination unchanged

v4_s10s.what_it_shows: Bank counter, worried customer, and a cheque crossed out in red.
v4_s10s.missing: Side-by-side diagram showing a cheque moving available deposits between accounts and credit payment creating a debt to repay.
v4_s10s.point: Cheque transfers existing deposits, subject to funds; Credit payment creates repayment debt

v4_s10b.what_it_shows: Cheque and credit-card icons with arrows, and a college icon with a green check; text says these are not currency.
v4_s10b.missing: A diagram separating payment acceptance from currency status, with dollar demand shown as an open question.
v4_s10b.point: Payment instruments do not confer currency status; Separate dimensions; dollar demand remains a question
